paper_a.title: Probability Inequalities for Sums of Bounded Random Variables (Hoeffding 1963)

paper_b.title: A Measure of Asymptotic Efficiency for Tests of a Hypothesis Based on the Sum of Observations (Chernoff 1952)

metadata.description: Hoeffding (1963) extends the MGF/Markov 'exponential trick' that Chernoff (1952) used to derive an abstract i.i.d. large-deviation bound P(S_n<=na) <= m(a)^n. Hoeffding inherits Chernoff's master technique (the 'Markov-exponential' inequality EP204.2 mirrors Chernoff's PSP205.1 / EP205.2) and pushes it in three directions Chernoff did not pursue: (i) explicit closed-form inequalities for sums of bounded variables (Theorems 1-3, including the now-canonical exp(-2 n^2 t^2 / sum (b_i-a_i)^2) bound and the variance-aware Bennett form), (ii) extensions to U-statistics, sampling without replacement, m-dependent sequences, and martingales, (iii) sharper one-variable MGF lemmas (Lemmas 1-3) tuned for boundedness rather than asymptotic efficiency. Chernoff's hypothesis-testing apparatus (asymptotic-efficiency index rho, likelihood-ratio Chernoff information, normal approximations) has no counterpart in Hoeffding, and Hoeffding's combinatorial/dependence extensions have no counterpart in Chernoff. Both papers are PDF-fallback extractions; LaTeX fidelity is reduced but node names and types are reliable.

matches.explanation: Hoeffding's 'Markov-exponential master bound' (EP204.2) is mathematically the same construction as Chernoff's Theorem 1 / 'Chernoff bound' (TP205.1, EP205.2): bound the indicator by exp(h(S-ES-nt)), take expectation, factor by independence, optimize over h. Hoeffding presents it as a master device feeding his Theorems 1-3, while Chernoff makes it the headline result. PSP205.1 in Chernoff's proof is the same Markov-exponential step (via the 'extended Tchebycheff inequality'). EP205.1 is Chernoff's definition of m(a)=inf_t e^{-ta}M(t), which is exactly the optimized form of Hoeffding's product after taking the n-th root. Hoeffding's EP204.11 (master bound for convex combinations) is the same Markov-exponential device extended via Jensen to convex combinations of independent-sum variables.

Hoeffding's Lemma 1 (LP204.1) is a one-variable MGF upper bound for a bounded random variable: E exp(hX) <= ((b-EX)/(b-a)) e^{ha} + ((EX-a)/(b-a)) e^{hb}. Chernoff's DP205.1 introduces M(t)=E(e^{tX}) and m(a)=inf_t e^{-ta}M(t) abstractly without restricting X. They play the same role (single-variable MGF object that the per-coordinate factorization of the Markov-exponential bound depends on), but Hoeffding instantiates it concretely for bounded X while Chernoff stays general.

Hoeffding's Lemma 2 (LP204.2) is the variance-aware analog of Lemma 1: E exp(hX) <= (b^2/(b^2+sigma^2)) e^{-(sigma^2/b)h} + (sigma^2/(b^2+sigma^2)) e^{bh} when EX=0, EX^2=sigma^2, X<=b. It plays the same single-variable MGF role as Chernoff's general M(t), specialized to a known second moment and one-sided boundedness. Chernoff has no closed-form analog because his interest is asymptotic rate, not closed-form bounds.

Hoeffding's Theorem 1 (TP204.3) gives three nested explicit upper bounds on Pr{X-bar - mu >= t} for X_i in [0,1]: a sharp binomial-type bound, an exp(-n t^2 g(mu)) refinement, and the famous exp(-2 n t^2). Chernoff's Theorem 1 (TP205.1) gives the abstract bound Pr{S_n <= na} <= m(a)^n for general i.i.d. X. Hoeffding's bound is the closed-form evaluation of m(a)^n in the Bernoulli/[0,1] case (the binomial extremum is explicit in RP204.2). EXT relationship: Hoeffding extends/specializes Chernoff's abstract rate to a usable closed-form inequality. EP204.3 (definition of g(mu)), EP204.5 (master expansion of G(t,mu)), EP204.6 (comparison ratios for the three bounds of Theorem 1), EP204.7 (identity relating G to g) and EP204.9 (convex envelope of e^{hx} on [a,b], the inequality behind Lemma 1) are all internal pieces of Theorem 1's closed-form machinery with no Chernoff counterpart.

Hoeffding's Theorem 2 (TP204.4) — 'Hoeffding's inequality' for sums of independent variables with possibly different ranges [a_i, b_i] — is an explicit-rate extension of Chernoff's TP205.1. Chernoff bounds Pr{S_n <= na} by m(a)^n with m(a) implicit; Hoeffding evaluates the master bound for arbitrary bounded ranges and obtains exp(-2 n^2 t^2 / sum (b_i - a_i)^2). The two theorems share the same underlying MGF/Markov machinery (PP204.2 explicitly invokes the Markov-exponential bound EP204.2).

Hoeffding's Theorem 3 (TP204.5; the variance-aware / Bennett form) is again a closed-form specialization of Chernoff's TP205.1, this time using both the upper bound b and the variance sigma^2 to sharpen the rate. The proof PP204.3 again routes through the Markov-exponential bound EP204.2 (= Chernoff's PSP205.1 step) but instantiates it via the more refined Lemma 2 (LP204.2). EP204.4 (extremal two-point distribution attaining (2.8)) and EP204.8 (comparison ratio B_1/B_2 between the (2.8) and (2.9) forms) are internal sharpness/comparison details with no Chernoff counterpart.

All three of Hoeffding's main proofs (PP204.1, PP204.2, PP204.3 for Theorems 1, 2, 3) share the same outer structure as Chernoff's PP205.1 upper-bound half: apply the Markov-exponential bound, factor by independence, optimize h. Chernoff's PP205.1 then continues with a multinomial / Stirling lower-bound argument and a discretization step (PSP205.2-PSP205.4) to establish the exact exponential rate, which Hoeffding does not pursue (he wants explicit upper bounds, not asymptotic tightness). Hence the proofs share their common ancestor (the upper-bound step PSP205.1) but diverge: Hoeffding plugs in his closed-form Lemmas 1, 2 and arithmetic-geometric / Taylor / Jensen estimates.

Composite L2 entry: in each of Hoeffding's three proofs the very first step (PSP204.1, PSP204.6, PSP204.9) is 'apply the Markov-exponential / exponential Markov inequality and a one-variable MGF lemma to each X_i'. This is the same step as Chernoff's PSP205.1 ('upper bound via extended Tchebycheff inequality'). Subsequent Hoeffding steps (AM-GM, optimization of h, Taylor's formula) realize the bound concretely, while Chernoff's subsequent steps (multinomial/Stirling lower bound, discretization) instead establish asymptotic tightness.

Both papers cite a Chebyshev/Tchebycheff inequality as motivation for the exponential Markov approach. Hoeffding cites the second-moment Bienayme-Chebyshev inequality as the weak-precursor bound; Chernoff cites the 'extended Tchebycheff inequality' (Markov on e^{tS_n}) attributed to Kolmogorov 1933. They are both external Markov-style citations that play the analogous role of motivating the exponential refinement, but they are different inequalities (second moment vs MGF).

Hoeffding cites Jensen's inequality / convex functions (DP204.2) as a tool, then uses it in PP204.3 / PSP204.10 (via Lemma 3's convexity of -f) to symmetrize over variances, and in PP204.4 / PSP204.15 to reduce sampling-with vs without replacement. Chernoff uses convexity of M(t) (Lemma 3 LP205.3, d^2M/dt^2 >= 0) to underwrite the existence of the optimizing t. Both papers lean on convexity but in different ways; this is a weak conceptual match.

Both papers open with the same notational setup: i.i.d. (or independent) X_1, ..., X_n, sum S_n = sum X_i, mean mu = E(S_n)/n, and (in Hoeffding) variance sigma^2. Chernoff additionally introduces the MGF M(t) and m(a). Same notation up to the choice of which moments / generating function to name.

Both papers open with the same target tail probability. Hoeffding writes Pr{X-bar - mu >= t} = Pr{S - ES >= nt}; Chernoff writes Pr{S_n <= na} (or >= na). The two are the same object up to recentering and the choice of upper vs lower tail.

Hoeffding cites Chebyshev's one-sided inequality as another second-moment baseline; Chernoff has no counterpart since he goes straight to the MGF/exponential approach. Skipping is not strictly required (this is an external-origin node), but the pair is interesting since both papers are in the same lineage of progressively sharper concentration inequalities.
Hoeffding cites Bennett's inequality (1962) as an alternative form of Theorem 3. Chernoff (1952) predates Bennett and has no analog.
Hoeffding cites Bernstein's inequality. Chernoff does not.
Hoeffding cites Prohorov's inequality (1959). Chernoff does not.
Hoeffding cites Doob's maximal inequality to extend Theorems 1-2 to martingales (RP204.4). Chernoff does not address martingales.
Hoeffding's corollary on the difference of two sample means is a direct application of Theorem 2; Chernoff has no analog (he is interested in asymptotic rates, not finite-sample two-sample bounds).

Hoeffding's tail bound for one-sample U-statistics (TP204.10), together with its supporting decompositions (EP204.10: T as a convex combination of dependent sums; EP204.12: U as average of independent-sum representations) — a major contribution — has no Chernoff counterpart. Chernoff's machinery is i.i.d. only.

Hoeffding's tail bound for sums of (r-1)-dependent variables (TP204.11), together with its definition of (r-1)-dependence (DP204.6) and the sum decomposition into r interleaved independent subsums (EP204.14), has no Chernoff counterpart.

Hoeffding's Theorem 4 (TP204.12; sampling without replacement is dominated by sampling with replacement under any continuous convex functional), its proof (PP204.4), the auxiliary 'sums related to U statistics' definition DP204.5, and the equation EP204.13 expressing W as a U-statistic with averaged kernel are all part of the convex-domination apparatus underlying Theorem 4, with no Chernoff counterpart.
Hoeffding's corollary deriving Theorems 1-3 bounds for sampling without replacement uses Theorem 4; no Chernoff analog.
Hoeffding's Lemma 3 (convexity of -f for the variance-aware MGF combination) is a paper-specific tool inside the proof of Theorem 3 with no Chernoff counterpart.

Chernoff's main problem statement — defining an asymptotic-efficiency index rho for tests that reject when the sum of observations falls below a threshold — has no Hoeffding counterpart. Hoeffding is interested in finite-sample concentration, not testing efficiency.

Chernoff's Lemma 1 (M(t) attains its minimum) is a structural fact about the MGF needed because Chernoff wants the optimum t*, not just a usable upper bound. Hoeffding does not need this — his Lemmas give explicit bounds without invoking optimum-attainment.
Chernoff's Lemma 2 (positivity of m(0) when X straddles zero) is internal MGF machinery for the rate analysis. No Hoeffding analog.
Chernoff's degenerate / one-sided MGF lemma is a technical edge-case for the rate function. No Hoeffding analog.
Chernoff's Lemma 6 (continuity / monotonicity of m(a)) is internal machinery for the rho-index analysis. No Hoeffding analog.
Notation specific to Chernoff's analysis of m(a) and t(a). No Hoeffding analog.

Chernoff's definition of the asymptotic-efficiency index rho (DP205.3, equation EP205.3: rho = inf_{mu_0<=a<=mu_1} max[m_0(a), m_1(a)]). No Hoeffding analog (Hoeffding does not address hypothesis testing).
Chernoff's definition of asymptotic relative efficiency e=log rho_1 / log rho_2. No Hoeffding analog.
Chernoff's Notation 5 (auxiliary expectations N(t), P(t), edges of MGF domain). No Hoeffding analog.
Chernoff's Notation 6 (log-likelihood-ratio statistic and its conditional MGFs). No Hoeffding analog — Hoeffding has no likelihood-ratio machinery.
Chernoff's Theorem 2 (rho governs inf_a (beta + lambda alpha) at the exact exponential rate). No Hoeffding analog.
Chernoff's Theorem 3 (efficiency interpretation of e). No Hoeffding analog.
Chernoff's Lemma 7 (derivative identities for m(a), t(a) via implicit function theorem). No Hoeffding analog.

Chernoff's Lemma 8 and the accompanying equation EP205.4 (the index of the likelihood-ratio test equals inf_{0<t<1} integral f_1^t f_0^{1-t} d nu — i.e., the Chernoff information formula now standard in information theory). No Hoeffding analog.
Chernoff's Theorem 4 (normal approximation of rho for likelihood-ratio tests). No Hoeffding analog.
Chernoff's Theorem 5 (normal approximation for general S_n tests when X is less efficient than the LR). No Hoeffding analog.
Chernoff's proofs of Theorems 2-5 (asymptotic-efficiency / normal-approximation analyses for hypothesis tests). No Hoeffding counterparts.
